**Joshua Kiprui Cheptegei** (born 12 September 1996) is a Ugandan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He is the current world record holder for the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), and once held the world-best time over the [15 kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15K_run "15K run") distance.

Cheptegei is the reigning [Olympic champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") in the 10000 m and three-time [World champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in the 10,000 m. Cheptegei also won a gold medal in the 5000 m and 10,000 m at the [2018 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2018_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2018 Commonwealth Games") and at the [2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). At the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), Cheptegei won gold in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"), becoming the Olympic champion and setting a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-5)
Cheptegei is the tenth man in history to hold the 5000 m and 10,000 m world records concurrently, both set in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-7)

Cheptegei was born on 12 September 1996 in Kapsewui, [Kapchorwa District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa_District "Kapchorwa District"), Uganda.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2) In primary school, he first played football and tried out [long jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_jump "Long jump") and [triple jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_jump "Triple jump"), but he switched to running when he discovered his talent in distance running.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2)
Cheptegei studied procurement and logistics management in Uganda and is employed by the [Uganda National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Police "Uganda National Police").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-8) His coach is Addy Ruiter. In the timeframe from March to May 2020, he reduced his weekly training sessions from 12 to 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

### 2015–2019: Career beginnings
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2015–2019: Career beginnings")]
[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg/330px-Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5,000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps,_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_(29090428856).jpg)
Cheptegei (L in yellow) races the 5000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), where he finished eighth.

### 2019–2020: World records
On 13 August 2020, a day before the [Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis") meet of the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") in Monaco, Cheptegei announced that he aimed to return to the track and run his first official race in the season with a world record time in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"), which would be more than 20 seconds faster than his personal best on a track.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-22) At the meet on the next day, with the help of expert pace-making from Roy Hoornweg, Stephen Kissa, and [Matthew Ramsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Ramsden "Matthew Ramsden"), he set a [new world record in the 5000 metres with a time of 12:35.36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres_world_record_progression "5000 metres world record progression"), which broke [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 16-year-old record—the longest duration in the history of the event—by almost 2 seconds.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-24) His splits were 2:31.87; 5:03.77; 7:35.14 and 10:05.46. Kenenisa congratulated Cheptegei from Addis Ababa.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

### 2019–2020: World records
On 7 October 2020, in Valencia, he set a [world-record time of 26:11.00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression") in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), which improved on [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 15-year-old record by more than 6 seconds.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-25)

### 2021–present: Olympic medals
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2021–present: Olympic medals")]
Cheptegei won gold in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and silver in the 10,000 metres at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-26)
At the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships"), Cheptegei won the 10,000 metres[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-27) and placed ninth in the 5000 metres.

Cheptegei studied procurement and logistics management in Uganda and is employed by the [Uganda National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Police "Uganda National Police").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-8) His coach is Addy Ruiter. In the timeframe from March to May 2020, he reduced his weekly training sessions from 12 to 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)
texts.15:
### 2015–2019: Career beginnings
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2015–2019: Career beginnings")]
[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg/330px-Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5,000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps,_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_(29090428856).jpg)
Cheptegei (L in yellow) races the 5000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), where he finished eighth.
texts.20:
### 2019–2020: World records
On 13 August 2020, a day before the [Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis") meet of the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") in Monaco, Cheptegei announced that he aimed to return to the track and run his first official race in the season with a world record time in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"), which would be more than 20 seconds faster than his personal best on a track.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-22) At the meet on the next day, with the help of expert pace-making from Roy Hoornweg, Stephen Kissa, and [Matthew Ramsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Ramsden "Matthew Ramsden"), he set a [new world record in the 5000 metres with a time of 12:35.36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres_world_record_progression "5000 metres world record progression"), which broke [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 16-year-old record—the longest duration in the history of the event—by almost 2 seconds.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-24) His splits were 2:31.87; 5:03.77; 7:35.14 and 10:05.46. Kenenisa congratulated Cheptegei from Addis Ababa.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)
texts.21:
### 2019–2020: World records
On 7 October 2020, in Valencia, he set a [world-record time of 26:11.00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression") in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), which improved on [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 15-year-old record by more than 6 seconds.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-25)
texts.22:
### 2021–present: Olympic medals
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2021–present: Olympic medals")]
Cheptegei won gold in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and silver in the 10,000 metres at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-26)
At the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships"), Cheptegei won the 10,000 metres[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-27) and placed ninth in the 5000 metres.

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)
Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.
At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)
Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.
The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwill_Games "Goodwill Games") over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barefoot_running "Barefoot running"). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics") and [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics").
In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)") in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idolatry "Idolatry") by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.
Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon") three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_International_Ladies_Marathon "Osaka International Ladies Marathon").

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egmond_Half_Marathon "Egmond Half Marathon") winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilburg_Ten_Miles "Tilburg Ten Miles"), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon") in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

texts.8:
Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)
Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.
At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.
texts.9:
[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)
Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.
The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.
texts.10:
In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwill_Games "Goodwill Games") over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barefoot_running "Barefoot running"). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics") and [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics").
In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)") in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idolatry "Idolatry") by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.
Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon") three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_International_Ladies_Marathon "Osaka International Ladies Marathon").
texts.11: Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egmond_Half_Marathon "Egmond Half Marathon") winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilburg_Ten_Miles "Tilburg Ten Miles"), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon") in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

# Loroupe honoured as Kenya's UN Person of the Year
[![Image 49: Facebook](https://worldathletics.org/static/facebook-white.png)](https://www.facebook.com/share.php?u=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya&title=Loroupe%20honoured%20as%20Kenya%27s%20UN%20Person%20of%20the%20Year "Share on Facebook")[![Image 50: Twitter](https://worldathletics.org/static/twitter-white.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya&text=loroupe-honoured-as-kenyas-un-person-of-the-year "Share on X")[![Image 51: Email](https://worldathletics.org/static/email-white.png)](mailto:?subject=Loroupe%20honoured%20as%20Kenya's%20UN%20Person%20of%20the%20Year&body=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya "Share via email")
Refugee Olympic Team Chef de Mission Tegla Loroupe (© Getty Images)
Tegla Loroupe has been honoured as the 2016 UN Person of the Year in Kenya for her work in ensuring the participation of the refugee team at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games.
Loroupe, a former marathon world record holder who won marathons in London, New York and Berlin in her heralded career, was the Chef de Mission for the ten-member squad that made up the Refugee Olympic Team, the first to compete at the Games.
Loroupe's journey with refugees began in 2014 when she took her peace-building efforts to refugee camps in Kenya where she discovered a great interest in athletics among refugee communities.

# Loroupe honoured as Kenya's UN Person of the Year
In 2015, she petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She then established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation. The Foundation is one of the projects which is supported by the IAAF's 'Athletics' for a Better World' social responsibility programme. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.
Her vision was realised this summer when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprised of ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Nairobi, Loroupe emphasised the role that each and every individual in the community plays to ensure there is peace. “We do not want to see more refugees," she said. "It does not help us. We want them to go back home and become ambassadors of peace."
The UNHCR Kenya Deputy Representative, Mr. Wella Kouyou, said Loroupe reminds us that refugees are human beings with capacity and aspirations just like anybody else.
“With her efforts, Tegla challenges all of us to also do our part in finding durable solutions for refugees," Kayou said.
**The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) for the IAAF**

Refugee Olympic Team Chef de Mission Tegla Loroupe (© Getty Images)
Tegla Loroupe has been honoured as the 2016 UN Person of the Year in Kenya for her work in ensuring the participation of the refugee team at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games.
Loroupe, a former marathon world record holder who won marathons in London, New York and Berlin in her heralded career, was the Chef de Mission for the ten-member squad that made up the Refugee Olympic Team, the first to compete at the Games.
Loroupe's journey with refugees began in 2014 when she took her peace-building efforts to refugee camps in Kenya where she discovered a great interest in athletics among refugee communities.

# Loroupe honoured as Kenya's UN Person of the Year
In 2015, she petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She then established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation. The Foundation is one of the projects which is supported by the IAAF's 'Athletics' for a Better World' social responsibility programme. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.
Her vision was realised this summer when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprised of ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.
Speaking at the award ceremony in Nairobi, Loroupe emphasised the role that each and every individual in the community plays to ensure there is peace. “We do not want to see more refugees," she said. "It does not help us. We want them to go back home and become ambassadors of peace."
The UNHCR Kenya Deputy Representative, Mr. Wella Kouyou, said Loroupe reminds us that refugees are human beings with capacity and aspirations just like anybody else.
“With her efforts, Tegla challenges all of us to also do our part in finding durable solutions for refugees," Kayou said.
